Cold came out of the stone like a bill. Isak knelt among the boxes, his palms burning where the corrugated cardboard had left red grooves. “The wall is sweating like a freezer. How am I supposed to stop the rest of the batch becoming mashed mango?”

Romy glanced briefly at the grey mortar from the doorway, then returned her attention to her phone. “Ask a builder, not me. I’m here to read meters.” She rattled her car keys and looked ready to leave.

Unfortunately, he persisted. “Builders want six weeks. There has to be a quick shield—plastic, salt, anything between the books and the stone.”

Romy lifted one shoulder. “The internet says to move the shelves. You have legs; try lifting.”

A box shook when he nudged it with his foot. “I tried. There’s no outlet anywhere else. I need something professional but affordable for a renter.”

“Ask the campus library technicians; they have desiccator bins.” She raised her espresso and found nothing but foam.

“They’re shut for refurbishment until January. Just give me one reliable tip and I’ll let you bolt.”

Her gaze went to the coffee-machine timer, which was already overtime. “The hardware aisle sells dehumidifier pots. Put two above and two below; problem solved.”

“They’ll spill when I move the boxes on Saturday. I need something that won’t leak.”

Her sigh clouded the window. “Vacuum-seal them in contractor bags and suck the air out with your mouth. You’ll shine with ingenuity.”

“Suck mould spores directly into my bronchi? No. Anything easier?”

Romy had reached halfway through the doorway, her coat grazing the frame. “If you want easy, sell the books and buy digital editions. Ten minutes, no damp.”

“I write in the margins; I can’t move off paper. Do NOT suggest libraries—I need my own copies here, not borrowed ones.”

“Bees ventilate their hives in summer by beating their wings two hundred thirty times a second; you could use airflow, not libraries.”

“Excuse me? I’m discussing fungus, not insects.”

She took a bee-shaped honey dipper from one of the boxes and watched it roll across the floor. “Keep the airflow. Leave a five-centimetre gap, the way bees leave space between layers of comb. Circulation prevents rot; it’s proven in Apis mellifera colonies.”

Isak’s notebook, its pages blistered, snapped shut. “Thanks, Apiarist Anonymous. Could you limit yourself to hygroscopic materials?”

“Bees gather propolis to coat the walls of their cavities; the thin resin layer resists microbes. Paint the backs of your shelves with that same enthusiasm.”

“Propolis resin on IKEA birch? Now you’re creating hobbies for me.”

“It’s only tree sap, and it’s cheaper than silica. Also, foragers signal distance with the angles of their waggle dances; you could aim a fan using the same kind of calibration.”

He gestured with his thumb toward the lone rotary fan, which buzzed like an intoxicated bumblebee. “Aim a fan, understood. Anything else before the mould graduates and writes its own dissertation?”

She looked at her watch one final time, firmly. “Queens keep the hive cohesive with pheromones. You could hang a lavender stick behind your books—the scent is antimicrobial and keeps both the pages and the workers calm.” Her keys chimed goodbye, and she left him with wet stone, an exhausted fan, and a faint, unbelievable smell of lavender in a place where no flower had ever grown.

Nerea’s shattered phone rested on the hatchback’s hood like a broken mirror, catching the flicker of the failing ceiling light. Practice chalk marked the concrete, while three minutes and five seconds of rooftop footage shone through the fractured screen. She only had to vanish for four beats without leaving any trace.

“Have you got a moment before you clock out?” she called, weaving between the idling van and the pillar. “I need an honest opinion on a single-take audition clip, and rumor has it you’re better at saying ‘cut’ than speaking English.”

Jareth already had both knuckles pale around the key fob. His hoodie was half zipped, and exhaust brushed against his shins. “If it’s a locked take, you’re finished, right? One take means there aren’t any cuts left to find.”

“The piece is three-oh-five, but the judges want three minutes exactly. Somewhere in it, I’m meant to disappear for four heartbeats.”

He rubbed at an imaginary itch beneath his cuff. “Four beats is easy—mute the backing track for two counts. That fades the problem into the floor.”

“That’s cheating. They’ll hear the gap in the drums. I need the dance to stay seamless, not the audio.”

“Then cut your landing after the barrel turn. People blink when they’re shocked anyway.”

Nerea moved between the bollards, one sock soaked by the gutter. “The landing has live sound—the foot hits concrete. You can’t punch that down. Try again.”

“Look, I’ll be on the clock soon. Go to the editing lab tomorrow; somebody there owes you favors twelve deep.”

She adjusted the speaker in her pocket, where 7/8 cymbals hissed like agitated cats. “The lab is booked until Thursday. You have the software on that crusty laptop in your van.”

His shoulders rose in a slow, delayed shrug. “The software is ancient, and the screen is cracked enough that you’d need tweezers to count the pixels. Take it to a real professional, yeah?”

“Five minutes in your van. I’ll bring the external drive and snacks; you drive, and I’ll trim it at red lights.”

“The red lights here last twenty seconds at most—barely long enough to connect the drive. You’ll only make yourself carsick.”

She pushed her fallen sneaker with a single bare toe, her jaw firm. “Then cut it for me now. Phone edit, free favor—I’ll owe you one back-row ticket forever.”

The van door opened with a sigh, sending out a breath of stale fries. “Make the deadline tomorrow, not tonight. Upload the raw version and call it ‘artistic restraint.’ Judges love the taste of ego.”

Nerea watched him climb inside as the door slammed, the sound traveling through the empty deck like a snare hit cut short too soon. Her thumb lingered over the cracked display: 3:05 in red. Somewhere inside that footage, the missing four beats were hiding behind sweat and concrete. She pulled her sock back on, switched off the speaker with her thumb, and began walking. The editing labs reopened Thursday; the upload was due Friday. If she couldn’t erase those seconds, she might still outrun them.

The senior center carried its usual December odor—radioactive cinnamon mixed with instant coffee that stained your tongue the shade of cheap carpet. Folding tables bowed beneath everyone’s nostalgia projects: cookie-cutter stars, battered pie tins, and the unavoidable pipe-cleaner candy cane. Gul bent over a six-inch square of roofing tin salvaged from a storm, sleeves pushed up, black fingerprints marking the places where the metal had resisted her. Across the vinyl snowflakes, Hristo held a leaking reindeer mug as cautiously as if it contained state secrets. The hair on his arms had turned silver, and pale scars climbed his forearms like ladders, each one a silent résumé from forty years of persuading sheet stock to cooperate.

Gul had no use for small talk. “I need it to reflect light like a mirror, but whenever I fold the edges, they stay sharp enough to cut someone. How do I correct that without dulling it?”

Hristo kept his eyes down. “You’re making one fold and stopping there. Fold it twice, a quarter inch inward, then flatten the seam using the hammer’s flat face. That removes the cutting edge and conceals the burr.”

One of Gul’s eyebrows gave a single impatient twitch. “Won’t that ruin the clean line? I’m making a snowflake, with details smaller than an eighth of an inch.”

Hristo smiled for the first time, faintly, like someone realizing he enjoyed the song playing on the radio. “The line will stay sharp if you score it first. Use the ball-peen to mark the inside score, then bend along that mark with needle-nose pliers. The metal obeys the rule instead of relying on your thumbs to guess.” He acted out the motion with empty hands, wrists relaxed, muscle memory quietly working.

Gul angled the tin, inspecting measurements only a calculus major would worry over. “And the reflection? The folded edge cuts off half the angle.”

“Put the fold on the back. The front remains flat.” Hristo struck the table twice to underline the point. “After folding, use a 320-grit sponge in gentle circles for six passes. It removes the microscopic burr and polishes the surface.”

“What can I do on the back without concealing the hammer texture?” Gul spoke in the fewest words possible.

“Don’t use the sponge over the textured areas.” Hristo took up a roll of blue painter’s tape and tore off a strip with absent-minded precision. “Mask the silhouette with painter’s tape, polish around it, then peel the tape away.”

He returned the roll, its loose end fluttering like surrender. Gul tapped her fingers against the table. “How long before the sponge clogs?”

“These tins destroy a cheap sponge after ten ornaments.” He shrugged with the practiced motion of someone who had once reset radial-arm saws. “Rinse it under hot water, rub it with your thumb, and let it dry for two minutes. It will be as good as new.”

Gul gave one brief nod. “Simple enough. Thanks—I thought I’d need to grind it.”

Hristo raised the reindeer mug in a gesture too smooth to be a toast and too purposeful to be dismissal. “Grinding removes tin thickness faster than rust. Keep the hammer singing and the tin will cooperate.”

At the front of the room, the glue guns began coughing awake. Neither of them headed that way yet; beneath the weary December light, the piece of tin in Gul’s hand was finally behaving.

Aminata’s mouse wheel cracked beneath her thumb again, producing the small, miserable click she had come to despise. Sixteen council districts, a single stakeholder pack, and three hours. She watched Spencer sweep past her desk, his backpack pulled high and his earbuds hanging loose like escaped IV tubes. Behind him, someone had written “SPENCER = SCRIPT GUY” on the whiteboard in permanent marker. She took it as an omen.

“Can you show me how to batch-export these maps? I have sixteen PDFs to produce by five.”

Spencer kept moving. “The scripting wiki is on SharePoint. Look there first; it’s pretty comprehensive.”

The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead like inexpensive cicadas. Aminata spun around and blocked the aisle. “I looked, but I couldn’t find the loop example for data-driven pages. Could you give me two minutes?”

He touched his watch. It read 3:11. “I’m literally on my way out. There’s a bus in four minutes. Sorry.”

She grabbed her laptop, its power cord trailing behind her. “Then walk with me to the plotter. You only need to tell me which toolbox contains the iterator.”

They moved past three desks, while Spencer searched for ways out. “I always used ModelBuilder, never Python. You’ll have to find someone who codes.”

“ModelBuilder is fine,” she said brightly, accepting the limitation. “Can you open your old model so I can copy it?”

Spencer stepped around the printer tray, where coffee was dripping onto outdated floodplain flyers. “It’s on the retired server. IT erased most of that material after the ransomware incident.”

Aminata gestured toward the whiteboard with her chin. “Really? You’re the only person listed there for automation.”

“The whiteboard is out of date. You should bug IT—policy says they keep backups.”

She felt the carpal tunnel in her wrist tapping out its tiny rhythm against her tendons. “IT takes two days to turn around a ticket. I need these maps tonight.”

Spencer arrived at the coat rack, drumming his fingers against the rubber-band ball he kept there. Snap, snap. A countdown. “Then export them manually. Fluorescent duct tape, right-click, repeat. It gets the job done.”

“That’s forty-eight clicks per run. My wrist is already buzzing.”

He swung the bag onto his shoulder, the bus ticket fluttering like a surrender flag. “Occupational hazard. Look, I really have to leave. Good luck.”

The door clicked shut behind him. Aminata looked at the bagel marked “Monday,” now a historical artifact. The plotter breathed out warm mechanical air over her ankles. She opened the SharePoint page again, her fingers suspended above the keys. Forty-eight clicks, repeated sixteen times. The overhead lights continued keeping score.

The fluorescent lights hummed above Selah like bargain-bin bees as she stood amid the drifting sawdust, her backpack pulling at her shoulders and toward the floor. She had come directly from the library, three books about colonial smuggling still pressing into her back, and now she was staring up at a lumber stack that seemed taller than her prospects for future earnings.

“Can I pick your brain about wood that won’t make a sliding lid jam?” she asked the man replenishing the off-cut bin.

The clerk stood upright, his navy cap the color of dishwater. “Sure. What size box?”

“Six by eight inches, with walls around half an inch thick.”

His pencil moved across a black notebook already tangled with numbers. “Use quartersawn cherry. It stays stable, cuts neatly, and won’t cost you a lung.”

She narrowed her eyes at the prices written in chalk. “How likely is it to warp?”

“Almost not at all if you seal the end grain. It’s for indoor use, right?”

“Yeah, a bedroom shelf.” Selah patted a maple plank. “Wouldn’t mahogany look richer?”

“Sapele is the cheaper cousin of mahogany. It looks fancy, but it shifts in summer. Go with cherry.”

She continued running her fingers over the boards, unable to keep them still. Graduation was twenty days away. The family brunch was in nineteen, with an empty place where her gift ought to be.

“I already have 240-grit sandpaper at home—is that enough?”

“Absolutely. Cherry burnishes at 240, so there’s no reason to pursue a glass finish.”

In the dim fluorescent light of aisle twelve, the caliper’s red handle caught her attention. She picked it up and squeezed the jaws open and shut repeatedly, like a mechanical crab. “Is there a trick to cutting the groove so the lid won’t catch?”

The clerk stopped, one hand resting on a short walnut off-cut that had no project waiting for it. “Make the groove just a little wider, then wax the tongue. Expansion needs room to breathe.”

“How much is ‘a little’?”

He pushed a business card between two piles of off-cuts. “Slide a playing card through. If it drags, take one more pass with the plane.”

The card moved easily. He nodded with satisfaction, the same way Victor would have reacted to a crossword clue he had solved in ink.

“What about the order for gluing it up?”

“Do the ends first and the long grain afterward. Put clamps every four inches; cherry is forgiving if you hurry.”

Selah breathed out. She returned the caliper to its hook. “Can twenty dollars cover the materials?”

“Easily. Cherry runs $6.40 per foot, and you only need half a foot. Take a scrap from the cart and you’ll save even more.”

She located a board roughly eight inches long, marked up but still usable. Half her pizza money survived. That evening she would pull the kitchen table into the middle of the room, open the windows so the sawdust could drift like snow, and sand until she made something slide open without catching.

Behind her, Victor went back to his notebook, already adding up board-feet for strangers who might never realize what good advice had cost.

Oksana drums one finger on the counter; a single Cyan fleck remains on her knuckle, a souvenir from the morning committee meeting, while “visually noisy” still seems to linger in the room. She studies the proof clipped inside the viewing booth, where the greens sag toward the color of spoiled mustard. “I need these greens to match the original litho, not this frog-bile nonsense.” Her delivery is brisk and clipped, with no interest in small talk.

Theocharis is partway into his backpack when he hears her. He pauses, thinking over the print head in the still air, then sets the bag down. Being helpful is easy when the problem is color rather than Wi-Fi. “Berwald is attempting green with just four inks. Begin with an IT8 scan and create a fresh profile.”

Oksana tosses her hair aside, wearing an expression that already says she was right. “I did that already. It’s still muddy.” Her tapping foot betrays a small surge of impatience.

“What illuminant setting?” he asks, rolling the spectrophotometer closer. The machine hums like a cat too indolent to purr.

“I left it on D50. Should I move it to D65?”

He angles the i1 and inspects its silver nose. “D65 is hotter; you’ll be wrestling with it for weeks. Limit the black point instead, to about L 12, then pull the midpoint back by three.”

“That will clip my shadows,” she says, tightening her jaw.

Theocharis disconnects the power cable and threads it through his fingers like a skipping rope. “Clipped is better than neon. The profile also works with the paper profile; which RIP?”

“ImagePrint.”

“Good. Turn off ‘absolute colorimetric’; it makes the spectro less obedient to white bumping.”

Oksana’s cursor springs across the nearby monitor, and the mouse click lands like punctuation. “Done. Where should I anchor the neutral foil? It’s adding blue.”

“Use a new reference file. Take the 30% gray patch, subtract 3 in ‘b’, and export the .ti1 again.”

She enters the values without glancing at the keys. “Three clicks south in ‘b’; the re-export is finished.” Sweat beads at her temple as the temperature-control lamp fills the sealed room with greenhouse heat.

He examines the i1 with an experienced fingertip. “Measure again, but let the i1 cool first—it gets chirpy when it’s warm.”

“How long?” She looks toward the wall clock, as if the minutes may have already escaped.

Theocharis picks up the metal cup of canned air and gives it a short white burst that disappears into mist. “Two minutes. You can squeeze the cup; don’t brew it like espresso.”

For the first time, she smiles, a small sign of relief. “I have two minutes. After the profile—test print first?”

“Yes, one 8×10 strip covering only the green range. Compare the south light first, then the booth.” He gestures toward the dusty louvers, the slats where sunlight still kneels beside them.

Oksana circles her shoulders as if unwinding cables. The committee meeting now seems far away. “And the certification form?”

Theocharis lifts his backpack onto one shoulder again, prepared for this final task. “Check ‘custom perceptual’ on the last line, add the date, and you’re covered.” He gives up the chair, and she takes the warmth he leaves behind.

Jasmina pushed a plastic chair toward Levent with her boot heel, its legs scraping loudly over the canvas floor. “I’m drowning in skin-temperature readings taken every second—how do I reduce that to one red flag for each firefighter?”

Levent steadied his laptop on one knee while the cooler beneath him rocked like an unwilling stool. “Start by calculating the rolling maximum across ninety-second windows, then flag anything more than two standard deviations above that person’s own pre-drill baseline. That gives you a binary go/no-go.”

She tapped the track pad, sending rows of data racing by. “Fine, but two sigma will catch half the crew during an Alabama summer. I need better specificity.”

He smiled, satisfied that the theory had survived contact with reality. “Easy—raise it to three sigma and require the trend to continue for three minutes; that should limit false positives unless the sun is actively trying to kill them.”

“Exactly, but post-exercise suppression muddies the baseline—how do I separate that out?”

Levent tapped her laptop lid. “Discard the first five minutes after they exit, and wait until heart rate falls below one-ten. Anything recorded after that is genuine heat load, not an anxiety spike.”

She wrote the note in neat, clipped letters. “That works, but trainees gulp water right away—skin temperature drops and then rebounds. How do I remove that artifact?”

“Label it a ‘cooling period’ and leave it out of the slope calculation; use the hydration timestamps as masks, expect the mean to return within two minutes, and ignore it.”

Jasmina looked toward a table where half-full cups stood in an uneven skyline. “I only logged water at the buckets, not every sip; there are some gaps in the data.”

“Interpolate between the hydration events you know about—linear is fine, this isn’t an ICU study—then mark the questionable windows with a low-confidence flag and review them manually later.”

The word manually tightened beneath her ribs. “Manual means me at two in the morning—I need a filter that automatically excludes obvious sensor drops, too.”

“Simple dropouts are readings that leap ten degrees in a single second—censor the surrounding five-second buffer, then use a majority vote from the three nearest sensors for the patch.”

She breathed out, claiming a small victory. “Great. Once the flags are clean, should I average them or use the worst episode from each shift?”

He leaned back with his hands on his thighs. “For the policy uplink, use the single worst sustained episode for each individual. Regulations prefer absolute peaks, not complicated averages.”

“Then the output is only that timestamp, the value, and the individual ID—one CSV line? Or JSON?”

“CSV, three columns. Chiefs open it in Excel like it’s sacred scripture. Send it nightly through sftp to the ‘Rehab Dashboard’ folder—it’s already whitelisted.”

“I can script that tonight; thanks, Levent. I owe you cold pizza.”

He shut the laptop, steam misting his glasses. “Make half of it vegetarian and we’re even; bring chips, too.”

She laughed, surprising both of them above the hiss of the leaking hose, and fastened the strap on her clipboard.

“That was emergency inventory salvage, a completely different animal.”

“Even so, you must remember whether the Riverfront branch crashed during the lunch rush. That’s useful information.”

The edge of her tote squeaked against the chair. “All I remember is that we ran out of jalapeños by Tuesday.”

He inhaled and kept his voice measured. “Look, if I show up Monday with no preparation, they’ll assign me to mop duty. Could you forward me even the old incident tickets?”

“I can’t access tickets. I’m literally limited to spreadsheets filled with apples.”

“Then tell me who actually owns menu deployment. I’ve been passed around like cold fries.”

She shrugged. “Honestly? Venue tech. But half of them are contractors, and the other half are at a conference in Vegas, hashtag sorry.”

Bastian leaned back, and the HDMI cable beneath his heel rasped over the tile. “So I’m supposed to wait until a taxi brings Colin back from McCarran? That’s a disaster plan.”

“Or pilot just one store, collect bullet points, and hope nobody complains.”

“One store restricts the data set; my professor wants variance across the full cohort.”

“Then take the downtown express bus to Systems and station yourself outside the server cage.”

“They’ll spot an intern wearing a lanyard and infrared badge and throw me out in three seconds.”

She rose, sending the chair rolling away. “Not my circus—I have a produce call in sixty seconds down in the loading bay.”

“One last thing—can I at least screenshot the last three months of hourly sales from your dashboard? That’s neutral territory.”

With her hand already on the door, she delivered one final deflection. “The dashboard wipes itself at the end of each cycle; there’s nothing to grab. Try Finance?”

Bastian watched the foamcore menus tremble above him and listened to the hallway echo with jalapeño crates being counted. He wondered whether anyone there cared about software half as much as they cared about vegetables.

The neighborhood grocer was a roomy walk-in closet, its strip light buzzing overhead while cilantro wilted in plastic. Low orange sunlight seeped through the windows. With Ramadan starting tomorrow, the tight aisles pulsed with customers pushing last-minute carts.

Yannis bumped the automatic door with his hip, his backpack knocking against his spine. He had twenty dollars, nine meals for breaking his fast, and ten minutes before the campus shuttle arrived. He took a battered basket and knocked it against his shoe: one, two, three.

Behind the counter, Ibtisam piled tins of ful like masonry, the brim of her cap shading her eyes. The clock told her there were forty-one minutes left—forty-one minutes of saying, “Sure, we have that,” before her ride could pull away from the curb.

Yannis approached, his basket rattling. “Excuse me—what’s the quickest filling thing I can cook after lab?”

“Get a can of ful; heat it, eat it, done.” She kept stacking the metal rectangles without looking up.

Dollar signs clicked through his mind. “I need to cover nine nights with twenty bucks; cans get expensive. Any bulk options?”

A carton landed with a thump. “Try the larger supermarket two blocks away; they sell sacks of lentils.”

“I’m walking, and the shuttle leaves in eight minutes. Anything here?”

She pushed the date rack toward him. “Rice and dates are discounted. They’re filling, cheap, and shelf stable.”

At midnight, plain rice sounded like damp gravel. “Plain rice? It takes forty minutes once I get home; that’s midnight.”

“Soak it while you’re working and finish it afterward. Or get instant if you’re that late.”

He remembered the instant rice from last week: white confetti stuck together with tap water. “Instant tastes like confetti. Is there a protein that cooks faster?”

She opened another carton with a pry. “Eggs, aisle three. Ask the cashier; I have boxes to unload.”

“Eggs will spoil if I buy them tonight and can’t cook them until after Ramadan begins.”

She rested the box’s edge on the shelf, already turning one shoulder away. “Then wait and shop tomorrow; the night hours are posted on the door.”

“I won’t get through my lab work before the shop closes. Help me make a plan now.”

A sigh escaped before she could hold it back. “Buddy, dates with peanut butter will keep you alive. Take it or leave it.”

Rice rasped around inside his head. He seized the closest box, its surface tacky against his palm. “Fine, dates. Is the two-kilo box cheaper per dirham?”

Ibtisam glanced at the clock—thirty-two minutes remained. “The price is on the sticker; the math is on your phone. I need to clock out.”

At last the basket stopped swaying. Yannis nodded—not in thanks so much as surrender, a treaty flagging defeat, and tucked the dates beneath his arm. The automatic door breathed him out into the orange light and the counting of stomachs.

Steam moved slowly over the gravel, carrying the smells of straw and used espresso into both their faces. Sofiane narrowed his eyes. The compost windrows shone like sleeping dragons, while his coil rig waited in their shadow for holes placed correctly according to some cold, exact numbers. Four hours of sleep had put sand behind his eyes, but caffeine kept jolting him awake.

He noticed the woman by the shipping-container doors. She held a guitar case in one hand, and her shoulders already angled toward the parking lot, like a weather vane set on escape. She seemed like the sort of person who either enjoyed hauling heavy objects or had stumbled into every mistake the farm could provide.

Sofiane moved into her path. “Morning—is it OK if I ask how you arranged the temperature probes when you tested the compost coils?”

“Wasn’t me. You want Li’s notes—the brown notebook in the lab.” She didn’t slow down. The guitar case swung beside her like a gate preparing to shut.

“I checked. There was nothing about probe spacing compared with pipe depth. I thought you might remember the intervals you used.”

She continued walking, her boots cracking the gravel. “Sorry, really not my project. Maybe the campus energy blog has the specifications.”

His laugh was mostly carbon dioxide. “The blog only says ‘thermistors appropriately zoned.’ That doesn’t tell me the actual distances. Five centimeters? Twenty?”

“It probably depends on the pile diameter. I’m catching a ride, so…” She glanced at a wristwatch that wasn’t there, yet the motion still communicated that she was late.

Urgency spread over his collarbones, echoing the heat rising from the compost rows. “Then give me a quick estimate—if the core reaches 60 Celsius and I need the gradient at the edge, would three sensors across thirty centimeters be enough?”

She shrugged, and the guitar case seemed to shrug too. “Sounds about right. Check Smits and Kirk, 2018—they explain thermal mapping in compost columns.”

“I’ve got another problem,” he said. “The journal is paywalled, and my access ran out yesterday. Could you just tell me the probe arrangement shown in Figure 4?”

She gave a small snort, part sympathetic and part annoyed. “I’d probably misquote it, mate. The library printer costs two bucks, and you can get a scanned copy in fifteen minutes.”

He raised the battered clipboard between them as though it were a peace flag. “I have coils to install today. I only need a rough sketch on the clipboard.”

She touched the board. “The clipboard is blank—wrong clipboard. Ask operations; the tool shed is beyond the tomatoes.” The steam shifted away, and briefly he caught the scent of her departure rather than compost: city shampoo and coffee cooling on a dashboard.

“Listen,” Sofiane said, his voice softer but still edged. “You’ve answered compost questions before, right? Hand to heart, can’t spare forty seconds?”

She backed away, already nearly at the asphalt. “Wish I could. Left my coffee cooling. Catch Li tonight—he’s working the five-to-midnight shift.” Then she disappeared, the guitar case carving a path through the smell of roasting grounds and someone else’s future data.

Sofiane watched the steam draw closed behind her like a curtain. The clipboard hung empty in his hand. Thirty centimeters. Three probes. Probably.

The bay stood half open as wind from the water pushed in the smells of diesel and the sharp metallic ticking of cooling welds. Jolene waited beside the stripped transit bus’s wheel well, her dented clipboard pressed to her coat like armor that had already failed her. Her advisor needed one page of heat-load figures by tomorrow, not a long explanation. Three online calculators had given her three different answers, all of them useless.

Sameer emerged from beneath the chassis on a creeper, tools rattling at his sides. A cold drop fell from the chrome chase overhead and slid down inside his collar. He looked from Jolene’s boots to her shivering posture and decided to answer quickly.

“Hey, sorry to interrupt—how do you even estimate the heat load for one of these trailers?”

“No problem. The rough formula is bodies, losses, and equipment. What’s the square footage?”

She read from her notes. “Twenty-eight by eight. There’s a window in the door, a tri-fold exam bench, and one small refrigerator.”

He rubbed his hands with a rag that could hardly have become any dirtier. “Begin with the envelope—the walls, roof, and floor. R-13 is typical here, so the U-value is about point-oh-seven-seven per square foot.”

Her pen paused above the page. “You’ve already lost me. Can you put it in BTUs?”

“Sure. The inside shell has roughly eight-twenty square feet of surface area. We use a thirty-degree delta-T—forty-five outside and a comfortable seventy-five inside. Eight-twenty times .077 times 30 comes to one-nine-hundred BTU.”

“That’s only the shell?”

“Only conduction through the materials. Then there’s infiltration. With a cheap door gasket, assume one air change per hour; that adds about another eight hundred BTU.”

She wrote rapidly. “So that brings us to twenty-seven hundred.”

“Plus the equipment. The fridge draws two-fifty watts while it runs, which adds another eight-fifty BTU.”

“Thirty-five fifty. Does the lighting count?”

“Six T8 LED tubes at thirty-five watts apiece. Add two-hundred more; it barely matters.”

Sameer moved a jack stand out of the way, and its clang rang through the bay. Jolene shifted her weight off one numb foot and onto the other. “People are the variable, right?”

“Yep. Two staff members and one patient, at five-hundred BTU of sensible load per body, gives fifteen hundred BTU. It can spike to twenty-two fifty while a stressed patient is inside.”

“What about solar load, with the sun beating on it?”

Sameer narrowed his eyes at the bare aluminum roof, which was already glaring in the low sunlight. “Solar depends on which wall faces south, the color, and how much shade there is. An unpainted aluminum roof like this gets nuked. We estimate three-hundred BTU per square foot at peak noon—the roof is two-twenty square feet—so that’s sixty-six hundred BTU baked in.”

“Crud. That puts us above ten thousand BTU installed.”

He gave her a small smile; he had already rounded the figures in his head. “The smallest mini-split that meets FDA clean-room spec is twelve thousand. That gives you room for a heatwave and a full waiting line.”

“So a fifteen-percent fudge factor is reasonable?”

“Fifteen is generous. Get the twelve K motor and sleep easy.”

At last, the clipboard stopped shaking. Jolene pulled off the top page, folded the calculations into her pocket like contraband, and walked toward the warm light of the office while the diesel-scented wind pressed against her back. Behind her, Sameer ducked beneath the bus’s ribs again, his tools clinking reassuringly against the ticking welds.
